opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the ideal people for this are a little unusual, because it sits at an awkward intersection. You need someone who's comfortable with the technical side, who understands machine learning well enough to have a feel for what's actually changing in capabilities and what's just hype. But you also need someone who's willing to think seriously about the messier social, economic, and political questions: how institutions respond, how incentives shift when human labor becomes less necessary, that kind of thing. Most people are trained in one of those and kind of allergic to the other.

So if I had to describe the person, it'd be someone with research experience, maybe a PhD student or postdoc, or someone from a forecasting or policy background who's picked up enough technical fluency. They'd need to be comfortable being wrong in public, because forecasting this stuff means making concrete predictions that will sometimes look silly in hindsight. And they'd need to resist the pull toward only answering questions that are easy to measure, because a lot of the most important questions here, like how much power ordinary people retain as AI gets more capable, are hard to operationalize.

I'd also say it probably shouldn't be just one person. Some of the best progress I've seen comes from small teams where one person is building the models and datasets and another is pushing on the conceptual framing and asking, "Is this even the right question?" Places like the forecasting organizations, some of the AI safety-adjacent think tanks, or even an academic lab with the right mandate could house it.

And if anyone listening thinks they might be that person, I'd genuinely encourage them to just start. Write up some forecasts, publish your reasoning, and reach out. The field is small enough that a few thoughtful people doing careful work can really move the conversation.

r002.rationale: It describes a suitable researcher or small team and possible host organizations, but does not recommend someone capable of building a substantial organization to take over the project.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm not sure it should be any one person — and I'd be a little suspicious of myself if I claimed to have a clean answer here. The project started almost by accident, out of frustration that so much of the discourse around AI timelines was either vibes or extrapolation from a handful of benchmark curves, and I wanted something more disciplined. But I'm a machine learning professor, not a forecaster, and I've run into the limits of what I can do on the side.

If I'm being concrete, the ideal person is someone who's genuinely comfortable in two worlds that don't usually overlap. They need enough technical fluency to actually read the papers and tell the difference between a real capability jump and a cherry-picked demo. But they also need the epistemic humility of a good superforecaster — someone who keeps score, updates when they're wrong, and doesn't fall in love with their own model. Those traits are weirdly anti-correlated in practice. The people with the deepest technical knowledge often have the strongest priors and the least interest in being graded.

So I'd rather hand it to a small group than an individual. Something like a grad student or postdoc with real ML chops paired with someone from the forecasting community — Metaculus, or one of the folks who came out of the Good Judgment world — plus a bit of institutional backing so it doesn't live and die on one person's attention span, which is frankly what happened with me. An organization like Epoch, or a group embedded at a university with some stable funding, would be more robust than a lone researcher.

The other thing I'd say is that whoever takes it over should feel free to throw out most of what I built. The important part isn't my particular set of questions or my aggregation scheme; it's the discipline of writing down falsifiable predictions and then actually checking them later. If someone else can do that better and more consistently than I did, that's the project succeeding, not failing.

r002.rationale: It favors a small group with institutional backing, but does not recommend a person who can build a substantial organization taking over.

astra-6.text: I’d love to see it taken on by a team with both machine learning expertise and experience in forecasting. You need people who can scrutinise the technical assumptions, but also people who will keep updating the forecasts and checking how well they’re doing. I don’t have a particular person in mind—it’s really that combination of skills and sustained attention that I’d be looking for.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a team with machine-learning and forecasting expertise, but does not mention using small models to bootstrap the project.

r002.rationale: The response does not recommend a person able to build a substantial organization; it describes a combination of skills and sustained attention.

sol-6.1.text: I think the ideal person would be someone who’s strong at both machine learning and forecasting, and who’s excited to make their assumptions explicit. A lot of the work is turning a vague story about how AI might develop into a model where people can inspect the assumptions, disagree with them, and see how that changes the forecast. So I’d be excited about someone who wanted to take ownership of that whole process, including making it useful to other people.
